scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

It's important to assess whether the investment is worthwhile, especially if the fabric won't be used again. 5. **Time Constraints**: Adequate time must be available to purchase the fabric, design an outfit, and have it made before the wedding. Time management is crucial to avoid stress. 6. **Alternative Options**: Exploring alternatives, such as matching colors or similar fabrics, could provide a compromise that respects family traditions while accommodating personal style. 7. **Communication**: Open dialogue with family members can help address concerns and find a compromise, ensuring participation without discomfort. 8. **Significance of the Event**: The wedding's importance to the couple should be considered, potentially outweighing personal inconveniences. 9. **Logistical Challenges**: The ease of sourcing the fabric is a practical consideration. Special ordering or difficulty in finding the fabric adds complexity. 10. **Long-term Use**: Considering future use of the fabric can help determine its value beyond the wedding. **Conclusion**: If the fabric is feasible and aligns reasonably with personal preferences, purchasing it could be a meaningful way to participate in the family tradition. message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for the sister to refuse to loan her brother her vacation money. Let me start by understanding the situation better. The sister is 21 years old, in her third year of university, and working to pay for her education. She's in business school, which she finds challenging but manageable. She's been saving money from her paychecks for a big vacation after she graduates, which is in about two years. The fund has $2,800 in it, and she's planning to use it for a cruise, a trip to Japan, or exploring different countries in Europe. Her brother is 30 years old and lives with their parents. He's in a bad job and decided to go back to school to improve his situation, which is why he moved back in with the family about a year and a half ago. The sister mentions that her brother is not good with money, makes about the same amount as her, but always seems to be broke. He doesn't buy groceries or pay rent, which is why the sister has been able to save up for her vacation fund. She buys most of her own groceries, pays for her makeup, health supplies, phone, and university fees. The brother has not been on a vacation in many years and has been hinting that he needs one. Their parents suggested that he could start saving now to afford a trip, maybe across the country in a year. Three days ago, the brother asked the sister if he could borrow her vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or fall. He argued that since she won't need the money for another two years, he would have plenty of time to pay her back. The sister refused, and her brother is now upset, arguing that it's unfair because, as the youngest child, she got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He also mentioned that she knew what she wanted to do for university the first time she went, whereas he had to go back, and that she's only been able to save so much money because "mom and dad spoiled her." The sister disagrees, stating that her father and her university classes taught her to budget, and she doesn't think her parents spoiled her. She believes her brother is more spoiled because he doesn't know how to handle real-world responsibilities outside his job. The sister feels it's unfair to have to give up her vacation money to her brother, and she doubts he will be able to pay her back in time. She's uncomfortable with the situation and is asking if she's "AITA" (Acting Inappropriately Towards Authority), which I think in this context means whether she's being unreasonable or unfair in refusing to lend her brother the money. Okay, so to determine whether it's right or wrong for the sister to refuse the loan, I need to consider several factors: 1. **Financial Responsibility**: The sister has been saving for her vacation for a reason, and it's a significant amount of money for her. She's planning to use it for a trip after she graduates, which is a goal she's been working towards. Her brother, on the other hand, has a history of being bad with money and is currently in a difficult financial situation. 2. **Family Dynamics**: The sister and her brother have different backgrounds and experiences. The sister feels that her brother is more spoiled and less responsible, which affects her willingness to lend him money. The brother feels that the sister has had more opportunities and support from their parents, which makes it unfair for her to refuse to help him now. 3. **Ability to Pay Back**: The sister is concerned that her brother won't be able to pay her back in time, especially since he's already struggling financially. This is a valid concern because if he can't pay her back, it could strain their relationship further. 4. **Alternative Solutions**: Instead of borrowing money from his sister, the brother could explore other ways to save for his trip. He could create a budget, cut unnecessary expenses, or look for additional income sources. The parents suggested he start saving now, which is a good approach. 5. **Emotional Impact**: The sister's refusal has caused tension between her and her brother. It's important to consider how this decision affects their relationship and whether there's a way to resolve the conflict amicably. 6. **Long-term Consequences**: If the sister lends her brother the money and he can't pay her back, it could lead to resentment and further financial strain. On the other hand, refusing to lend him the money might lead to immediate conflict but could prevent longer-term issues. 7. **Personal Boundaries**: The sister has the right to protect her financial goals and personal boundaries. It's important for her to stand her ground if she feels that lending the money would compromise her future plans. 8. **Communication**: Open and honest communication between the sister and her brother could help resolve the issue. The sister could explain her reasons for refusing the loan and listen to her brother's perspective, potentially finding a middle ground. 9. **Role of Parents**: The parents have already suggested that the brother start saving, which is a responsible approach. The sister could encourage her brother to follow through on that advice rather than relying on her savings. 10. **Fairness and Equality**: The sister feels that her brother is being unfair in his accusations, and she has valid points about her own financial responsibility and the support she's received. It's important to assess whether the situation is truly unfair or if it's a matter of differing perspectives on fairness. Considering all these factors, it seems that the sister's decision to refuse the loan is reasonable. She has a valid concern about her brother's ability to pay her back, and she has been responsible in saving for her own future plans. While it's important to support family members, it's also crucial to protect one's own financial well-being. The sister could communicate her concerns clearly to her brother and suggest alternative ways for him to save for his trip, but it's not unreasonable for her to refuse the loan under the circumstances.
